newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-HK handover reminds Goa of Portuguese rule.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-HK handover reminds Goa of Portuguese rule.

text.p: China's pledge to maintain Hong Kong's separate identity has struck an eerie chord in Goa.
It took India 14 years after itself gaining independence from British rule in 1947 to reclaim Goa, and New Delhi promised to maintain the distinct identify of the "colony within a colony".

For people in Goa, dotted with palm-fringed beaches and shacks dispensing a potent cashewnut liquor called "feni", the Goa beloved of the 1960s hippie generation, the real issue is their cultural identity.
Afonso de Albuquerque seized Goa in 1510, making the outpost on India's west coast one of the most important ports in maritime history.
In 1530 Goa was declared the capital of Portugal's Eastern Empire. It was dubbed the Rome of the East.
But no empire lasts forever.
LIBERATION, INVASION, OR CONQUEST?
When the Indian army marched into Goa on December 16, 1961 it encountered little resistance from the Portuguese who had ruled the idyllic enclave for four and a half centuries.
For some Goans this event represented "liberation". For others it was an "invasion". Several years later India's Supreme Court held that it was a "conquest".

In 1962 the then Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru said: "We have made it clear that we want Goa to maintain its separate identity, separate individuality, call it what you will, because in the course of more than 400 years, Goa has had a separate identity and the course of history has imparted it some."
But Goans, who spoke their native Konkani language and were equally fluent in Portuguese, were soon swamped by India's throbbing democracy.
For decades Goa's northern neighbour, the Indian state of Maharashtra, tried strenuously to get the stubborn little federally-ruled territory to merge with it.
The "pro-mergerists" tried to drive a wedge between Goa's Catholics and the majority Hindus and branded Goans opposed to absorption by Maharashtra as "pro-Portuguese".
An overwhelming 81 percent of Goans voted in a historic Opinion Poll in 1967 on the merger question, and a majority chose to maintain their separate status.
MERGER ISSUE STILL GENERATES PASSION
Three decades later Goa is a proud state in the Indian Union, but the merger issue is still a political hot potato.

The debate is fuelled by Goans' ambivalence about their cultural debt to the Portuguese, and local newspapers run columns on whether or not India should join the commemoration of Vasco da Gama's discovery of the sea route to India in 1498.
"The most unique legacy left to Goa by the Portuguese was a uniform civil code," says M.S. Usgaocar, a Goan and India's Additional Solicitor General.
Such a code is a model for the rest of India, divided by different laws of inheritance, marriage and family rights among the nation's Hindus, Moslems and Christians.
Nearly five centuries of Portuguese rule have left their indelible stamp on Goa's language, customs and traditions. Most Goans consider themselves to be Goan first and Indian second.

"I am a Goan, born and raised as a Portuguese citizen. I was not made an Indian at the point of a gun but acquired Indian nationality voluntarily by renouncing my Portuguese citizenship, because Goa means the world to me," said Leonor Rangel-Ribeiro, a former UN expert in community development.
GOANS WERE "INDIAN" JUST AS SWISS ARE "EUROPEAN"
"We existed as Portuguese India before India existed as a nation. Yet, we felt we were Indian in the same way the French, Germans or Swiss feel they are European," Rangel-Ribeiro said.
Goans see a parallel in the failure of China and Britain to grant Hong Kong self-determination about its status.
"Neither the Indians nor the Portuguese consulted us on what we wanted. The ideal and democratic option was never given to us -- that of self-determination," Rangel-Ribeiro said.
Most Goans simply wish to live in peace.
But the state's breathtaking landscape, resplendent architecture and gracious way of living are under siege.
Bailon de Sa, president of the Menezes Braganca Institute, attributes the crisis to apathy among Goan youth.
"They have no vision, no wish to do something for Goa, no love for Goa," he said, adding that India's failure to protect Goa's heritage had robbed the young of a passion for their homeland.
Older Goans fret that economic progress has not been kind to their home.

"One would question the establishment of industries that have no economic justification, especially those that disrupt our ecology, disfigure our scenery and create social problems like slums...The day is not far off before we reduce Goa to a ghost town," says educationist Ravindra Kelkar.
